title: Parameters from concentration versus time data

segs.text: Module two, objective three. Calculating parameters from concentration versus time data. Given a dose and one or two measured plasma concentrations, you work out the patient's elimination rate constant, half-life, starting concentration, volume of distribution and clearance. Each value feeds the next, so the order matters: k first, then half-life, then C zero, then V D, then clearance and amounts. Compare like with like. A rate constant comes from two amounts or from two concentrations, never from an amount and a concentration together. V D is the converter between the two, because an amount equals V D times a concentration.

card.m: k → t½ → C<sub>0</sub> → V<sub>D</sub> → Cl<sub>T</sub>, amounts
k from two amounts or two concentrations, never mixed

segs.text: The rate constant k equals l n C one minus l n C two, divided by t two minus t one. With amounts, k equals l n D zero minus l n D B, divided by t. Either way k is in per hour, and it is the slope of l n C p against time with the sign changed. Half-life equals zero point six nine three divided by k. Per hour in the bottom leaves hours. This line is not on the equation sheet, and she named it as one to memorise. It is the same at any concentration for a first order drug.

When no sample was taken at time zero, C zero equals C t times e to the k t, where C t is a measured concentration at time t. The exponent is positive because you are going back in time, so C zero must be higher than every sampled point. For an amount rather than a concentration, D B equals D zero times e to the minus k t, or D B equals V D times C t. Both routes give the same answer, and she accepts either.

card.m: +kt: back in time, C<sub>0</sub> above every point
D<sub>B</sub> = D<sub>0</sub>e<sup>−kt</sup>   or   D<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>D</sub> × C<sub>t</sub>

segs.text: Her deck practice. A two hundred milligram I V dose is given to an eighty kilogram man. At six hours the plasma level is fifteen milligrams per liter, and V D is ten percent of body weight. Find the amount in the body at twelve hours, and the half-life. First convert V D to liters, using one liter per kilogram: zero point one zero times eighty kilograms is eight liters. Next, turn the six hour concentration into an amount, so it can be compared with the two hundred milligram dose. D B equals eight liters times fifteen milligrams per liter, which is one hundred twenty milligrams, because liters cancel and milligrams remain.

card.m: C = 15 mg/L at 6 hr; V<sub>D</sub> = 10% of body weight
D<sub>B</sub> = 8 L × 15 mg/L = 120 mg at 6 hr

segs.text: Now k comes from the two amounts. k equals l n two hundred minus l n one hundred twenty, divided by six hours, which is zero point zero eight five per hour. The amount at twelve hours is D zero times e to the minus k t. That is two hundred milligrams times e to the minus zero point zero eight five times twelve. The exponential is zero point three six, so the amount is seventy two milligrams.

The half-life is zero point six nine three divided by zero point zero eight five per hour, which is eight point one five hours. Carrying k unrounded, at zero point zero eight five one four per hour, gives eight point one four hours. The seventy two milligrams is the same either way. Her added question asks the concentration at twelve hours. Seventy two milligrams divided by eight liters is nine milligrams per liter.

Her review problem. A one hundred fifty four pound woman gets a fifteen milligram per kilogram I V bolus. Levels are thirty two point eight five micrograms per milliliter at two hours, and nine point three two micrograms per milliliter at eight hours. Both are concentrations, so k comes straight from them. l n thirty two point eight five minus l n nine point three two is one point two five nine eight. The points are eight minus two, six hours apart. One point two five nine eight divided by six hours gives k of zero point two one per hour. The half-life is zero point six nine three over zero point two one per hour, which is three point three hours.

card.m: 32.85 mcg/mL at 2 hr; 9.32 mcg/mL at 8 hr

segs.text: The dose needs the weight in kilograms. One kilogram is two point two pounds, so one hundred fifty four pounds divided by two point two is seventy kilograms. Fifteen milligrams per kilogram times seventy kilograms is one thousand fifty milligrams. Next, run back to time zero: C zero equals thirty two point eight five times e to the zero point two one times two, which is fifty micrograms per milliliter. That is fifty milligrams per liter, because micrograms per milliliter and milligrams per liter are the same number. Then V D is one thousand fifty milligrams over fifty milligrams per liter, which is twenty one liters.

Last, clearance is k times V D. Zero point two one per hour times twenty one liters is four point four one liters per hour. Her questions run as one patient and a chain of small parts, from k and half-life through C zero, V D and clearance to an amount at a stated hour. Fifteen minutes must be converted to zero point two five hours, and ninety nine point nine percent eliminated always means ten half-lives. Weight in pounds with a milligram per kilogram dose tests the two point two conversion, and every later part depends on it. The usual trap is dividing the dose by a concentration to get k. Convert one first, so both are amounts or both are concentrations.
